**Summary.** This paper reports on distributing light-matter quantum correlations using a highly multiplexed solid-state quantum memory array. By leveraging both spatial and temporal multiplexing, the authors achieved quantum correlations in up to 60 modes and demonstrated a significant rate enhancement for quantum communication over a metropolitan fiber link. This work advances the feasibility of long-distance quantum networks.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the physical implementation challenges of quantum networking by demonstrating high-rate entanglement distribution using solid-state memories, which is crucial for scaling quantum communication infrastructure.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge addressed is overcoming the fundamental rate limitation in long-distance quantum repeater architectures imposed by classical signaling time.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrated light-matter quantum correlations in 60 spatio-temporal modes and achieved a 60-fold enhancement in the correlated telecom photon detection rate by utilizing multiplexing over a metropolitan fiber link.

**Method.** Quantum correlations were distributed and measured using a time-multiplexed solid-state quantum memory array (QMA) coupled with a cSPDC source, and the resulting idler photons were sent over a 39.1 km fiber link.

**Model / system.** The system uses a quantum memory array based on a Pr3+:Y2SiO5 crystal, employing both spatial (10 cells) and temporal (up to 6 modes/cell) multiplexing via the full atomic frequency comb protocol.

**Key observables.** Cross-correlations ($g^{(2)}_{s,i}$), coincidence rates ($R_C$), and the rate enhancement factor.

**Important parameters / regimes.** 39.1 km fiber link length, 60 spatio-temporal modes, $393 \mu	ext{s}$ round-trip communication time.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The experiment operates in a realistic scenario where the generation rate is limited by the round-trip communication time.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the experimental setup, the temporal sequence of photon storage across multiple memory cells, and plots showing cross-correlations and the rate enhancement vs. the number of modes.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the experimental setup, the protocol for storing and retrieving photons in the multiplexed QMA, the measurement of quantum correlations both locally and over a long-distance fiber link, and the quantitative analysis of rate enhancement.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Multiplexed quantum memories increase the entanglement distribution rate in long-distance quantum repeater architectures by harnessing storage in several degrees of freedom. Here, we report on the distribution of light-matter quantum correlations using an array of time-multiplexed solid-state quantum memories. We store telecom-heralded single photons sequentially in up to ten memory cells using the full atomic frequency comb protocol with on-demand read-out in a Pr$^{3+}$:Y$_2$SiO$_5$ crystal. Leveraging both spatial and temporal multiplexing, we demonstrate quantum correlations between the telecom photon and up to 60 spatio-temporal modes of the quantum memory array. We then transmit the heralding telecom photon over 39.1 km of deployed optical fiber in the Metropolitan Area of Barcelona. In a realistic scenario where the generation rate is limited by the two-way communication time, we show that up to 15 % of the $393 μs$ round-trip communication time is filled with communication trials, leading to a 60-fold enhancement in the rate of detected telecom photons correlated with the quantum memory array, compared to a single-mode memory. With increased storage times and efficiencies, our multiplexed quantum memory array will constitute the backbone of a long-distance quantum network, establishing remote entanglement at high rates.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a comprehensive theory for controlling a harmonic oscillator using feedback derived from quantum-limited position measurements. It quantifies the fundamental trade-off between damping the oscillator's motion and amplifying measurement noise. The results provide concrete, bandwidth-dependent design rules for achieving optimal quantum cooling and sensing performance.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant to AMO and quantum optics as it provides rigorous theoretical tools for designing quantum feedback loops, which are crucial for cooling and sensing in modern quantum technologies.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the optimal measurement-based feedback control strategy for a damped harmonic oscillator, balancing the goal of mechanical stabilization against the unavoidable amplification of quantum measurement noise.

**Main result.** The analysis derives an analytic design rule for optimal feedback gain, showing that achieving positive near-resonant damping requires the product of the controller cutoff and measurement bandwidth to exceed the square of the mechanical resonance frequency.

**Method.** The authors use a combination of classical and quantum Langevin equations, analyzing the closed-loop displacement spectrum by separating the response into damping and noise reinjection components.

**Model / system.** The system is a damped harmonic oscillator, applicable to optomechanical or interferometric sensors, subjected to feedback derived from a quantum-limited position measurement.

**Key observables.** Effective occupation number ($n_{eff}$), closed-loop displacement spectrum ($S_{xx}(\omega)$), and the total force noise spectrum ($	ext{S}_{	ext{tot}}^F(\omega)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Mechanical decay rate ($\gamma_u$), feedback gain ($\gamma_{	ext{fb}}$), controller roll-off frequency ($\omega_f$), and measurement bandwidth ($\omega_{	ext{meas}}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the imprecision–backaction constraint ($	ext{Imp} \cdot S_{ba}^F \geq \hbar^2/4\eta$) and often uses near-resonant approximations, which are shown to be dependent on bandwidths.

**Figures summary.** The notes mention a dimensionless map of the gain-optimized high-Q occupation and comparisons between near-resonant and full-spectrum calculations.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from a classical formulation to the quantum extension, deriving the closed-loop spectrum, separating damping and noise terms, establishing the necessary bandwidth conditions for damping, and concluding with an optimization map.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study measurement-based feedback control of a damped harmonic oscillator, motivated by optomechanical and interferometric position measurements, in which feedback is synthesized from a displacement measurement. For a band-limited derivative controller, the loop shapes the mechanical susceptibility and reinjects measurement noise, creating a tradeoff between stabilization and noise amplification. We present a compact classical formulation that isolates this tradeoff in the closed-loop displacement spectrum and identifies the parameters governing resonance suppression versus noise-driven actuation. We then extend the same topology to a quantum-limited position detector, enforcing the imprecision-backaction constraint and introducing finite measurement bandwidth that regularizes high-frequency noise reinjection and adds phase lag in the feedback path. In the high-$Q$ regime we obtain an analytic design rule for the optimal feedback gain at fixed controller and measurement bandwidths and compare it with full-spectrum calculations. The comparison shows that a high mechanical quality factor alone does not guarantee quantitative agreement: the accuracy of the near-resonant approximation depends strongly on the controller and measurement bandwidths. Because finite measurement bandwidth changes both the magnitude and phase of the feedback loop, the analysis separates the near-resonant damping contribution from imprecision-noise reinjection and shows that positive near-resonant feedback damping requires the product of the controller cutoff and measurement bandwidth to exceed the square of the mechanical resonance frequency. Finally, we present a dimensionless map of the gain-optimized high-$Q$ occupation and compare its predictions with full-spectrum optimization. All analytical gains evaluated in this map satisfy the full closed-loop stability criterion for these parameters.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper analyzes the consistency of describing Maxwell-Cattaneo charge transport using a Schwinger-Keldysh effective field theory. The authors find that incorporating intrinsic dissipation fundamentally changes the entropy conservation laws. By enforcing modified KMS symmetry, they derive new constraints on the transport coefficients, providing a rigorous framework for non-equilibrium quantum hydrodynamics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work connects non-equilibrium statistical mechanics (entropy production, KMS symmetry) with advanced field theory techniques (Schwinger-Keldysh) to model dissipative transport, which is crucial for understanding open quantum systems dynamics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the conditions under which the nonlinear Maxwell-Cattaneo theory of charge transport can be consistently embedded into a local Gaussian Schwinger-Keldysh effective field theory while maintaining a modified dynamical KMS symmetry.

**Main result.** Treating the additional vector field as intrinsically dissipative fundamentally alters the entropy-current analysis, requiring independent supply of entropy-current improvements beyond what is fixed by the hydrostatic generating functional.

**Method.** The authors employ the Schwinger-Keldysh formalism to construct stochastic effective theories, analyzing entropy current divergences and imposing constraints derived from the modified KMS transformation.

**Model / system.** The system models charge transport governed by the Maxwell-Cattaneo theory, which extends standard diffusion by incorporating a relaxation mode ($\zeta_\mu$). The analysis is performed within the framework of U(1) gauge invariance and stochastic field theory.

**Key observables.** The entropy current ($\mathcal{S}_\mu^{	ext{can}}$) and its divergence ($
abla_\mu S^\mu$), which must be non-negative on-shell, are key diagnostics.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The relaxation time ($	au$) and the structure of the constitutive relations (e.g., Langevin canonical form parameters) are important.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the assumption that the modified KMS transformation is a symmetry of the action, and that field redefinitions are local and invertible.

**Figures summary.** No specific figures are described, but the notes reference tables detailing discrete and intrinsic PT assignments for the enlarged field space.

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by first establishing the entropy current analysis for the Maxwell-Cattaneo model, then deriving constitutive relations in a Langevin canonical form, and finally using KMS symmetry constraints to analyze ambiguities and ensure thermodynamic consistency.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We determine the conditions under which the nonlinear Maxwell-Cattaneo theory of charge transport admits a local Gaussian Schwinger-Keldysh embedding with a particular modified dynamical KMS symmetry. We show that treating the additional vector as intrinsically dissipative fundamentally modifies the entropy-current analysis: the hydrostatic generating functional no longer fixes all entropy-current improvements, which must instead be supplied independently. Subsequently we discuss the additional constraints not contained in the hydrodynamic analysis that are imposed by the modified KMS transformation becoming a symmetry of the action. We both interpret and supply the corresponding stochastic quasi-hydrodynamics.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents a novel broadband Purcell filter for superconducting qubits that resolves the conflict between fast quantum operations and qubit coherence. By engineering the filter with distinct notches and a dedicated reset stub, the authors achieve coherence times over 1 ms while maintaining fast readout and reset capabilities. This provides a critical hardware advancement for scalable quantum computation.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses hardware limitations in superconducting quantum computing by providing a scalable, engineered solution to the Purcell decay problem, which is crucial for building fault-tolerant quantum processors.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Accelerating qubit reset and readout operations for Quantum Error Correction (QEC) typically increases qubit decay via the Purcell effect, creating a fundamental trade-off.

**Main result.** The authors designed a broadband Purcell filter that decouples reset and readout paths, achieving Purcell-limited coherence times exceeding 1 ms over 1.2 GHz while enabling fast (100 ns) reset and 500 ns readout.

**Method.** The work involves designing and experimentally implementing a superconducting microwave filter structure incorporating intrinsic and bandstop notches, alongside dedicated reset resonators.

**Model / system.** The system uses superconducting qubits coupled to a microwave filter on a flip-chip processor. The architecture utilizes engineered notches and a dedicated reset stub to create a low-frequency reset mode, allowing independent optimization of the readout and reset channels.

**Key observables.** Purcell-limited relaxation time ($T_{1,P}$), readout time (500 ns), reset time (100 ns), and dephasing suppression factor (70).

**Important parameters / regimes.** 1 ms coherence time over 1.2 GHz bandwidth; 99.6% reset efficiency; $\kappa-\chi$ mismatch for dephasing suppression.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that decoupling the reset and readout paths via engineered filter components can resolve the inherent trade-off between speed and coherence.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the physical layout and circuit schematic of the filter, the measured transmission spectrum showing the protected bands, and characterization plots comparing measured $T_1$ to the theoretical Purcell-limited lifetime.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by identifying the Purcell decay problem, proposing a broadband filter architecture with decoupled reset/readout paths, detailing the experimental implementation and characterization of the filter's spectral properties, and finally presenting measurements demonstrating fast, high-fidelity operations alongside long coherence times.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Rapid reset and readout of qubit states are essential for quantum error correction, yet accelerating these operations through stronger coupling to a dissipative environment inevitably increases qubit decay via the Purcell effect. Here we present a broadband Purcell filter that decouples the reset and readout paths, enabling both operations to be independently optimized without compromising qubit coherence. The filter employs two engineered notches - an intrinsic notch and a bandstop notch - to provide broadband Purcell protection, together with an additional reset stub that creates a reset mode below the protected band. To enable fast reset while suppressing filter-mediated interactions between qubits, we couple each qubit to a dedicated reset resonator. We experimentally demonstrate Purcell-limited relaxation times exceeding 1 ms across a 1.2 GHz bandwidth, simultaneously with 500 ns readout without a Josephson parametric amplifier and 100 ns reset with 99.6% efficiency. The reset resonator is designed with a deliberate kappa-chi mismatch, which suppresses photon-shot-noise-induced dephasing by a factor of 70 compared to the readout resonator. Our work provides a scalable hardware solution that resolves the traditional trade-off between fast qubit operations and qubit protection, advancing the prospects for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents an experimental demonstration of a high-rate, multipartite quantum secret sharing protocol designed to resist sophisticated participant attacks. By generating and distributing four-qubit GHZ states over a fiber network, the authors achieved a measurable secret key rate and calculated a substantial finite-key lower bound. This work advances the practical feasibility of secure quantum communication for multiple untrusted parties.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it pushes the boundaries of experimental quantum networking by demonstrating high-rate, secure multi-user quantum key distribution, which is a core component of future quantum internet infrastructure.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of implementing high-rate multipartite quantum secret sharing (QSS) protocols that maintain composable security, specifically overcoming vulnerabilities in canonical GHZ-based schemes to participant attacks.

**Main result.** The authors experimentally demonstrated a QSS protocol achieving a high asymptotic secret key rate of $750 \pm 10$ bits per second, yielding a projected finite-key lower bound of 8.7 Mbits over 24 hours.

**Method.** The protocol was experimentally evaluated using a discrete-variable (n, n)-threshold QSS scheme implemented with photonic GHZ states, followed by a finite-key analysis to quantify extractable secure key length.

**Model / system.** The physical system involves generating four-qubit GHZ states using two domain-engineered entangled photon pair sources pumped by a pulsed laser via SPDC in AKTP crystals. The state is then distributed across a 4-arm star network emulating 20 km of fiber.

**Key observables.** Maximum generation rate ($\approx 5025$ counts/s), asymptotic secret key rate ($750 \pm 10$ bits/s), and the finite-key lower bound (8.7 Mbits).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The security analysis relies on the composable trace-distance sense ($\epsilon_{	ext{sec}}$) and involves optimizing the measurement basis probability ($p^*_{key}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The finite-key analysis assumes that the measured source and device statistics remain stationary over the entire execution period.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the QSS protocol steps (state distribution, basis reconciliation, key encryption). Figure 2 details the experimental setup using pulsed lasers, EPS, and fiber transmission. Figure 3 and 7 relate to the finite-key analysis and error tracking over distance.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the theoretical framework for composable security in QSS, presents the experimental setup for generating and distributing GHZ states, measures key rates and error statistics, and concludes with a finite-key analysis to quantify the extractable secret key length.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Future quantum communication networks will conceivably support cryptographic tasks that require entanglement among more than two users. Quantum secret sharing is a prime example where entanglement provides a direct means to coordinate untrusted parties with security from eavesdropping in a multi-party setting. However, the canonical GHZ-based protocols can be vulnerable to participant attacks, in which untrusted parties try to learn the secret without collaborating. Here, we experimentally evaluate a discrete-variable $(n,n)$-threshold quantum secret-sharing protocol whose finite-key analysis provides composable security against general attacks, including participant attacks. Using two domain-engineered entangled photon pair sources, we generate 4-qubit GHZ states at rates above $5\times10^3$ fourfold events per second and a maximum asymptotic secret key rate of $750 \pm 10$ bits per second. We then distribute the state through a 4-arm star network comprising 20km of fibre in total. From the measured event rates and error statistics, we infer that a randomised 24-hour execution with the optimised basis probability would yield a composable finite-key lower bound of 8.7 Mbits, under the assumption that the measured source and device statistics remain stationary.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reports on the opto-electrical detection of donor bound excitons in silicon-on-insulator (SOI) substrates, establishing a pathway for spin readout. By measuring spectral shifts and linewidths in samples of varying thickness, the authors confirm that the spin-sensitive transition survives integration into nanoscale devices. This work is vital for advancing solid-state quantum computing platforms.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the physical realization of solid-state qubits by demonstrating a robust, optically addressable, and electrically readable spin system in a scalable platform (SOI), which is crucial for quantum computing architectures.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The goal is to establish a scalable opto-electrical pathway for reading out the spin state of donor electron spins in silicon, moving from bulk samples to integrated Silicon-on-Insulator (SOI) platforms.

**Main result.** The donor bound exciton (D^0X) transition is successfully detected in SOI substrates, showing measurable spectral shifts and broadening compared to bulk, confirming the viability of the electrical readout mechanism in integrated devices.

**Method.** The experiment uses tunable diode lasers to excite D^0X transitions in samples of varying thickness on SOI, measuring the resulting laser-induced photoconductivity change at cryogenic temperatures.

**Model / system.** The system involves donor bound excitons in silicon, whose spin state is highly coherent. The analysis utilizes the Pikus-Bir Hamiltonian to model strain effects on the valence band and the Zeeman Hamiltonian for spin splitting.

**Key observables.** Exciton resonance wavelength, transition linewidth ($\Gamma$), and the energy shifts caused by strain components ($\epsilon_{ij}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Device layer thickness (e.g., $1 \mu	ext{m}$ vs. $300 	ext{ nm}$), magnetic field strength (up to $400 	ext{ mT}$), and strain tensor components.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that the observed spectral shifts are dominated by strain effects, and that Fabry-Pérot interference can be accurately removed via Fourier domain filtering.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare exciton spectra across different silicon samples (FZ, CZ, SOI A, B, C), illustrating the spectral shifts and broadening observed in the SOI structures relative to bulk measurements.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first demonstrating the feasibility of the measurement on different SOI samples (A, B, C), then quantitatively analyzing the spectral shifts and linewidths to attribute them to strain, and finally detailing the Hamiltonian framework used to model the strain-dependent energy levels.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Spin of a donor bound electron in silicon has been shown to be a very coherent qubit system but lacks a coherent optical interface. There does, however, exist a donor bound exciton transition that can be excited optically but decays dominantly via an Auger recombination producing an electrical signal. This provides an opto-electrical pathway for spin readout. Scaling this readout to single-spin level will require interfacing the spins with silicon photonics for efficient guiding of photons, which in turn will require moving to silicon-on-insulator (SOI) substrates. Here we demonstrate first ensemble opto-electronic measurements of donor bound excitons in SOI material, including isotopically purified 28-Si device layers. The experiments show pronounced shifts in the resonance wavelengths and broadenings of the transition linewidths compared to the bulk experiments.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reports on the realization and characterization of an all-van-der-Waals superconducting qubit using a NbSe2-hBN-NbSe2 junction. By employing cQED techniques, the authors measured coherence times comparable to established superconducting qubits. The work is significant because it proves that vdW heterostructures can form compact, high-performance qubits for quantum information processing.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the hardware challenge in quantum computing by demonstrating a viable, scalable material platform (vdW heterostructures) for superconducting qubits, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems research.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to develop superconducting qubits using van der Waals (vdW) materials to create compact, low-loss, and scalable quantum devices.

**Main result.** The all-vdW qubit achieved coherence times comparable to conventional Al-AlOx-Al qubits while offering a reduced device footprint due to the merged-element geometry.

**Method.** The study employed circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) techniques, including spectroscopy, Rabi oscillations, and Ramsey/Hahn-echo measurements, to characterize the qubit performance.

**Model / system.** The system is an all-vdW superconducting qubit based on a NbSe2-hBN-NbSe2 junction, modeled using the Cooper-pair-box Hamiltonian. The hBN layer acts as both the Josephson coupler and the shunt capacitor.

**Key observables.** Average energy-relaxation time ($T_{1,\mathrm{avg}} = 55 \mu	ext{s}$), Hahn-echo coherence time ($T_{2\mathrm{E},\mathrm{avg}} = 21 \mu	ext{s}$), and Ramsey coherence time ($T_{2\mathrm{R},\mathrm{avg}} = 1.9 \mu	ext{s}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Josephson energy ($E_J/h = 4.29 	ext{ GHz}$), Charging energy ($E_C/h = 0.13 	ext{ GHz}$), and the ratio $E_J/E_C \approx 33$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The relatively low Ramsey time is attributed to enhanced sensitivity to charge noise rather than being a fundamental limitation of the platform.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 details the fabrication process and circuit layout. Figure 2 presents spectroscopy and Rabi oscillation measurements used for characterization.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the fabrication of the all-vdW qubit, characterizes its superconducting parameters using cQED techniques, measures key coherence times ($T_1, T_2$), and analyzes the sources of dephasing limitations.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Advances in solid-state physics, materials science, and device engineering have accelerated the development of superconducting qubits. Among emerging platforms, van der Waals (vdW) materials and their heterostructures are potentially attractive building blocks for quantum devices, yet their realization in qubit architectures remains largely underexplored. Here we report an all-vdW superconducting qubit based on a NbSe$_2$-hBN-NbSe$_2$ junction, in which a thin hBN layer simultaneously provides Josephson coupling and capacitive shunting between two NbSe$_2$ islands, forming a "merged-element" transmon. Temporal characterization using circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) techniques yields an average energy-relaxation time $T_{1,\mathrm{avg}} = 55 ~μs$, Hahn-echo coherence time $T_{2\mathrm{E},\mathrm{avg}} = 21 ~μs$, and Ramsey coherence time $T_{2\mathrm{R},\mathrm{avg}} = 1.9~μs$. The relatively low Ramsey time is primarily attributable to an enhanced sensitivity to charge noise consistent with the realized device parameters and not a fundamental limitation. These results show that lumped-element superconducting qubits based on vdW heterostructures can achieve coherence times comparable to those of conventional Al-AlO$_\mathrm{x}$-Al qubits, while offering a reduced device footprint and suppressed stray capacitive coupling.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper shows that the superior performance of Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interferometry, typically associated with quantum entanglement, can be achieved using simple frequency product states. By employing post-selection measurements, the authors demonstrate that the essential resource is effective frequency anti-correlation, not entanglement itself. This offers a more practical physical mechanism for high-precision quantum sensing.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a crucial theoretical insight into the necessary quantum resources for high-precision sensing, suggesting that spectral correlations alone can mimic entanglement-enhanced performance in specific physical setups.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To demonstrate that the metrological advantages of Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference can be achieved without relying on quantum entanglement.

**Main result.** The key metrological advantages (dispersion cancellation, wide dynamic range) are reproduced using frequency product states and post-selection, showing the resource is effective frequency anti-correlation, not entanglement.

**Method.** The authors compare the coincidence probability derived from entangled states versus product states, utilizing post-selection measurements and analyzing the resulting Fisher Information.

**Model / system.** The system involves Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference measurements using either spectrally entangled biphoton states (from SPDC) or frequency product states as the input probe.

**Key observables.** Coincidence probability $P_c(\omega, \omega')$, Quantum Fisher Information ($F_Q$), and Classical Fisher Information ($F_{cl,post}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Spectral width ($\sigma$), sample delay ($	au$), and dispersion coefficients ($eta_2$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method relies on post-selection to extract anti-diagonal components, and the analysis of noise uses first-order phase noise approximations.

**Figures summary.** Figures simulate the spectral correlation map $P_c(\omega, \omega')$ showing the anti-diagonal selection line, and the resulting Fourier transform in the spatial domain, confirming the reproduction of the HOM interference pattern.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the conventional entangled HOM scheme, then proposes and analyzes the product-state scheme, demonstrating the reproduction of key features like peak narrowing and dispersion robustness, and finally compares the ultimate precision limits using Fisher Information.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference in the multimode frequency domain has been widely used in precision metrology, benefiting from robustness against dispersion and phase noise, as well as a large dynamic range and compatibility with fragile samples. Conventional multimode HOM metrology exploits frequency-entangled states, which naturally satisfy bosonic exchange symmetry under any centered symmetric joint spectral distribution, to provide these advantages. However, these entangled states are typically generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC), requiring strong pump lasers that hinder practical implementation. In this paper, we employ frequency product states, which do not possess entanglement or path-mode exchange symmetry, as the probe state and post-select measurement outcomes exhibiting frequency anti-correlation. Our results demonstrate that these metrological advantages arise neither from entanglement nor from bosonic exchange symmetry, but rather from spectral anti-correlation

</details>

**Summary.** This experiment investigates noise limitations in Si/SiGe spin qubits by comparing coherence at a specially engineered 'decoherence sweet spot' versus a neighboring site. By minimizing the coupling between charge noise and qubit frequency, the researchers achieved significantly longer coherence times. The residual noise spectrum at the sweet spot strongly matches theoretical predictions for $^{29}	ext{Si}$ nuclear spin noise, confirming the effectiveness of sweet-spot operation.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides crucial experimental validation of noise mitigation techniques in solid-state qubits, demonstrating how engineering the physical environment (finding a sweet spot) can suppress environmental coupling mechanisms, which is vital for scaling quantum processors.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to characterize and mitigate residual noise sources that limit the coherence time of electron spin qubits in Si/SiGe heterostructures.

**Main result.** Operating the qubit at a 'decoherence sweet spot' significantly suppresses the coupling between charge noise and qubit frequency noise, bringing residual noise levels close to the fundamental limit set by $^{29}	ext{Si}$ nuclear spin fluctuations.

**Method.** Coherence times ($T_2^*$, $T_2^{	ext{CPMG}}$) and noise power spectral densities (PSDs) are measured by comparing qubits at different locations relative to the local electric field gradient.

**Model / system.** The system uses electron spin qubits in $^{28}	ext{Si/SiGe}$ quantum dots, where coherence is limited by the transduction of charge noise via the local stray field gradient. The analysis compares measurements at a sweet spot (low gradient) versus a neighboring site (high gradient).

**Key observables.** Coherence times ($T_2^*$, $T_2^{	ext{CPMG}}$), Frequency Noise Power Spectral Density $S(f)$, and Qubit-sensor cross-correlation strength $r_i(f)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Residual $^{29}	ext{Si}$ concentration ($\approx 800$ ppm), Sweet Spot condition (minimal field gradient), and frequency noise spectral shape ($1/f^2$ decay).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The noise analysis often relies on approximations for noise extraction from CPMG sequences and the assumption of mutual uncorrelation between different noise sources for cross-correlation analysis.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the comparison of coherence times and noise spectra between qubits at different gradient regimes, showing the dramatic improvement at the sweet spot and matching the predicted nuclear spin noise spectrum.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically compares coherence measurements (Ramsey/CPMG) between two neighboring qubits, quantifies the reduction in noise susceptibility at the sweet spot, and finally performs detailed noise spectroscopy to identify the residual noise source as $^{29}	ext{Si}$ nuclear spin fluctuations.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In $^{28}$Si/SiGe spin qubits with micromagnets, the longitudinal stray field gradient transduces charge noise into qubit frequency noise and limits coherence. We compare two neighboring qubits in the same device with 800 ppm residual $^{29}$Si, one near a decoherence sweet spot where the gradient is locally minimized and the other at a position with a larger gradient. At the sweet spot, $T_2^*$ reaches 67 $μ\mathrm{s}$ and the Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill coherence time reaches 4.6 ms, whereas $T_2^*$ is 5.2 $μ\mathrm{s}$ at the neighboring qubit. Near 1 Hz, the frequency noise power spectral density at the sweet spot is nearly two orders of magnitude lower than at the neighboring qubit. The magnitude and low-frequency decay of the residual spectrum are compatible with the prediction for $^{29}$Si nuclear spin noise, and the weak interqubit correlation indicates that local noise becomes important for dephasing at the sweet spot. Despite a finite correlation with the charge sensor, sweet-spot operation strongly reduced the transduction of charge noise, bringing the residual frequency noise close to the level predicted for $^{29}$Si nuclear spin fluctuations.

</details>

**Summary.** This work presents a method to create fast, tunable two-qubit quantum gates in superconducting qubits by exploiting Landau-Zener interference. The technique is highly advantageous because it allows for continuous control frequency tuning and fast gate speeds. Furthermore, the protocol can be extended to multiplex multiple couplers, demonstrating robust control over quantum interactions.

**Why it may be interesting.** The use of non-adiabatic dynamics (LZ interference) to engineer controlled interactions is a powerful technique applicable across quantum optics and open quantum systems, providing an alternative to standard dispersive coupling methods.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper proposes and demonstrates a novel method for implementing high-fidelity two-qubit quantum gates in superconducting circuits using quantum interference effects.

**Main result.** The Landau-Zener (LZ) interference mechanism enables fast, tunable two-qubit gates, which are locally equivalent to an iSWAP gate, and this method supports multiplexing control for multiple couplers.

**Method.** The gates are realized by periodically modulating the coupler frequency to induce consecutive Landau-Zener transitions, which are modeled as a sequence of Mach-Zehnder interferometers.

**Model / system.** The system involves superconducting qubits (transmons/flux qubits) coupled via a tunable coupler qubit, described by a time-dependent Hamiltonian. The analysis extends to include leakage channels (qutrits) and decoherence effects.

**Key observables.** Gate fidelity, population swap fidelity, on-off ratio ($\eta$), and the data qubit oscillation frequency ($\Omega$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The control frequency tunability (up to hundreds of MHz), the coupling strength ($g$), and the coherence times ($T_1, T_\phi$) of the qubits.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The model uses approximations like the adiabatic impulse model and assumes Markovian evolution for decoherence analysis; leakage channels are modeled using an effective qutrit Hamiltonian.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the LZ interferometer sequence, the Bloch sphere evolution, simulated population oscillations showing the gate action, and finally, the fidelity and on-off ratio for multiplexed couplers.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from introducing the LZ gate mechanism via interference (analogous to Mach-Zehnder interferometers) to analyzing the gate's performance, including leakage suppression and demonstrating the capability for multiplexing multiple couplers.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We propose and demonstrate gates between two superconducting qubits based on quantum interference of consecutive Landau-Zener (LZ) transitions. This gate mechanism bridges between baseband and parametric two-qubit control, enabling in situ tuning of the control frequency across a continuous interval up to hundreds of MHz. Another advantage compared to dispersive couplers is that the speed of the LZ gate is on the order of the full coupling strength. We experimentally demonstrate the gate on two platforms, a modular chiplet architecture of coupled generalized flux qubits, and on a monolithic transmon architecture. The combination of tunability and gate speed establishes the LZ gate as a unique tool for multiplexing control pulses and interconnecting superconducting chiplet architectures.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reports the experimental realization of automated geometry theorem proving on a superconducting quantum processor. The authors developed quantum frameworks for both algebraic deduction (using quantum pseudo-division) and symbolic reasoning. By successfully proving known geometry theorems, they establish that complex logical reasoning is a viable near-term task for quantum hardware.

**Why it may be interesting.** While the core application is mathematical logic, the paper provides a concrete, hardware-level demonstration of executing complex, structured quantum algorithms (like QPD) on near-term superconducting devices, which is highly relevant for quantum algorithm development.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To experimentally demonstrate automated theorem proving, specifically for geometry theorems, using quantum computation.

**Main result.** The authors successfully proved two geometry theorems, including the perpendicularity of a square's diagonals, on a superconducting quantum processor.

**Method.** They developed two quantum frameworks: one using quantum pseudo-division for algebraic deduction and another using a hybrid quantum-classical approach for symbolic proof search.

**Model / system.** The work is performed on a fully programmable superconducting quantum processor featuring 121 frequency-tunable transmon qubits arranged in an $11 	imes 11$ lattice.

**Key observables.** Measurement probabilities corresponding to the successful deduction of zero remainders (algebraic proof) or the coherent generation of a proof sequence (symbolic search).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Gate fidelities (e.g., two-qubit gates $>99\%$), circuit depth (e.g., 77 layers for QPD step 1), and the number of qubits used (up to 28 physical qubits in optimized circuits).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The process assumes that geometric relations can be mapped exactly into formal polynomial or full-angle quantum representations, and that hardware imperfections can be mitigated via techniques like Pauli Twirling.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the superconducting processor architecture, the workflow for both algebraic (QPD) and symbolic proof search, and detailed circuit diagrams showing the implementation of complex gates and the final experimental point-value correspondence.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the theoretical foundations of quantum theorem proving, presents the two complementary quantum frameworks (algebraic and symbolic), describes the complex quantum circuit compilation and optimization process required for the superconducting hardware, and concludes with experimental results proving specific geometry theorems.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Automated theorem proving seeks to use computational systems to prove or disprove mathematical and logical statements [1, 2]. It underpins a wide range of applications, and enhancing theorem-proving capabilities remains a central objective in artificial intelligence [3]. Although recent neuro-symbolic systems have achieved remarkable progress [4-7], their operation is ultimately constrained by classical computational architectures. Quantum computing [8], by contrast, enables information encoding and coherent parallelism beyond classical limits [9-14], raising the possibility of accelerating structured symbolic deduction [15]. Here we report the experimental realization of automated geometry theorem proving on a fully programmable superconducting quantum processor. We develop two complementary quantum proving frameworks. The first implements Wu's algebraic elimination method using quantum pseudo-division, with multivariate polynomials represented in superposition states, enabling quantum algebraic theorem proving. The second implements the full-angle method as backward symbolic reasoning through a hybrid quantum strategy-guided architecture, demonstrating a general route toward quantum symbolic proof search. As illustrative examples, we prove two theorems on a superconducting quantum processor: the perpendicularity of the diagonals of a square and a 1978 International Mathematical Olympiad geometry problem. Our results establish, at the experimental level, automated logical reasoning as a viable task for near-term quantum processors and provide a concrete pathway toward quantum-enhanced symbolic intelligence.

</details>

**Summary.** This research demonstrates a breakthrough in solid-state quantum memory by storing multi-qubit entanglement at room temperature using a silicon carbide quantum node. By coherently transferring quantum information from a fast electron spin to much longer-lived nuclear spins, the entanglement lifetime is extended by over two orders of magnitude. This establishes SiC color centers as a powerful, scalable platform for quantum computing and sensing.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, scalable solid-state architecture for quantum memory by decoupling fast control operations from long-term storage, which is highly relevant for building quantum processors.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central challenge addressed is achieving robust, long-lived entanglement storage at room temperature in solid-state quantum systems.

**Main result.** The authors successfully demonstrated room-temperature storage of multi-qubit entanglement by coherently transferring quantum correlations from a fast electron spin processor to long-lived nuclear-spin memory qubits.

**Method.** The process involves using tailored microwave/RF pulse sequences and a SWAP-gate protocol to map the entangled state from the electron-nuclear subsystem onto the nuclear spins.

**Model / system.** The platform is a shallow single PL6 color center in 4H-SiC, forming a hybrid three-qubit register (one electron spin, two coupled $^{29}	ext{Si}$ nuclear spins). The system dynamics are governed by the hyperfine interaction Hamiltonian.

**Key observables.** Fidelity of generated states (e.g., Bell state: $94\pm2 \%$; GHZ state: $89\pm4 \%$), and the extended entanglement lifetime ($\sim 244 \mu	ext{s}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Room temperature operation, electron-spin coherence time ($T_{2e}^* \approx 1.75 \mu	ext{s}$), and nuclear-spin coherence time ($T_{2n}^* \approx 359 \mu	ext{s}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The storage lifetime is limited by residual electron-mediated decoherence, and the approach assumes the natural availability of multi-nuclear-spin registers in SiC.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the energy levels of the three-qubit register, ODMR spectra confirming control, and density matrix reconstructions showing the successful transfer and decay of entanglement over time.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem (decoherence), details the physical system (PL6 in SiC), describes the measurement techniques (ODMR, QST), presents the core protocol (SWAP-gate transfer), and concludes by demonstrating high-fidelity, long-lived entanglement storage in both homonuclear and heteronuclear registers.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Robust entanglement at room temperature is a central challenge for solid-state quantum information processing and quantum-enhanced sensing. Here we demonstrate room-temperature storage of entanglement in a silicon carbide (SiC) quantum node by coherently transferring an electron-nuclear entangled state onto long-lived nuclear-spin memory qubits. Using a shallow single color center in 4H-SiC, conventionally denoted PL6, we realize a fully addressable three-qubit register composed of one electron-spin processor and two strongly coupled $^{29}$Si nuclear-spin memory qubits. This platform enables the deterministic generation of high-fidelity entangled states, including a nuclear-spin Bell state with a fidelity of $94 \pm 2\%$ and a three-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ)-type state with a fidelity of $89 \pm 4\%$. By implementing a SWAP-gate protocol in the strong hyperfine-coupling regime, the electron-nuclear entanglement is transferred to the nuclear-spin memory with a fidelity of $92.5 \pm 2.5\%$, extending the entanglement lifetime by a factor of 240. We further confirm the generality of this approach in an additional heterogeneous $^{29}$Si-$^{13}$C nuclear-spin register and, through a statistical survey of 200 single PL6 centers, show that multi-nuclear-spin registers occur naturally with probabilities above 10%. These results position shallow SiC color centers as a powerful platform for entanglement-assisted quantum sensing and scalable room-temperature quantum technologies.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper investigates optimizing QAOA parameters on real quantum hardware by comparing batched versus sequential optimization strategies. It demonstrates that grouping multiple parameter evaluations into a single job (batching) drastically reduces the impact of job submission overhead compared to running evaluations one by one. This highlights that optimizing the classical optimization loop is as critical as optimizing the quantum circuit itself.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it addresses the practical, non-algorithmic overheads (job scheduling, communication latency) that dominate near-term quantum computation, which is crucial for any physicist designing quantum algorithms for real hardware.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper compares the efficiency of batched versus sequential optimization strategies for finding optimal parameters in the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA). The core challenge addressed is minimizing the overhead associated with submitting jobs to cloud-accessed quantum hardware.

**Main result.** The batched pattern search method significantly outperforms sequential optimizers like COBYLA by amortizing the constant job submission overhead across multiple parameter evaluations, reaching comparable parameter quality in fewer total jobs.

**Method.** The authors implemented and compared two optimization routines: a batched pattern search that submits multiple parameter sets in one job, and COBYLA, which requires a separate job for each function evaluation.

**Model / system.** The problem solved is the cardinality-constrained portfolio selection, formulated as a QUBO solvable via QAOA. The experiments are conducted on IBM's ibmfez quantum processor, utilizing a custom odd–even transposition network to realize the required couplings deterministically.

**Key observables.** Parameter quality (e.g., approximation ratio, CVaR), number of submitted jobs, and total shots.

**Important parameters / regimes.** QAOA depth ($p$), number of assets ($n=6, 8, 10, 12$), and the optimization cost function ($	ext{CVaR}_\alpha$ with $\alpha=0.5$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The comparison is limited by the job submission overhead, which is assumed to be constant regardless of the number of circuits in the job. The small instance sizes allow for exact classical verification of the optimum.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare resource usage (gate count, depth, time) between custom synthesis and preset pass managers, and show convergence curves comparing the two optimization methods.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the problem context (QAOA optimization on noisy hardware) and the overhead challenge. It then details the comparison between batched and serial optimization methods using portfolio selection as a benchmark. Results show performance gains for batching, followed by a depth scan confirming optimal QAOA layers.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

On a cloud-accessed quantum processor the classical optimizer of a variational algorithm communicates with the device through submitted jobs, and each job carries a queueing and turnaround overhead that does not depend on how many circuits it contains. We study a simple consequence of this for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA). An optimizer whose next set of trial parameters is known before any result returns can evaluate the whole set in one job, whereas a sequential optimizer such as COBYLA spends one job per function evaluation. We compare a batched pattern search with COBYLA on IBM's \ibmfez\ processor for cardinality-constrained portfolio selection with six to twelve assets, giving both optimizers the same number of jobs and the same number of shots. At every size the batched search reaches, after its first job, a parameter quality that the serial optimizer takes several jobs to match, and the two methods converge to comparable final values; repeating the eight-asset comparison from four starting points gives the same ordering each time. The instances are small enough to be solved exactly, which lets us check that the device's output distribution is correlated with the true ranking of portfolios and is clearly separated from a control circuit of the same depth with the cost layer removed. A short scan over circuit depth at classically optimal parameters shows that on this device the measured solution quality peaks at two or three QAOA layers. The protocol is described in enough detail to be reproduced, and the notebooks and raw counts are released.

</details>

**Authors:** Xiang Li, Yong Wang, Lijun Liu, Yiguang Hong, Qing Gao, Shuming Cheng  
**Type:** both · **Category:** quantum information and computing · **PDF:** <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.15662v1>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a novel, efficient protocol for Quantum State Tomography (QST) by leveraging Kirkwood-Dirac (KD) quasiprobability. It significantly reduces measurement overhead by requiring only two complementary measurements and employs a specialized complex logistic regression estimator. The results demonstrate that this method allows for the rapid, high-fidelity reconstruction of large, mixed-state quantum systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, scalable algorithm for characterizing complex quantum states, which is foundational knowledge for designing and benchmarking quantum hardware.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Quantum State Tomography (QST) is crucial for characterizing quantum systems, but standard methods suffer from exponential measurement and computational costs.

**Main result.** The proposed KD-based protocol significantly reduces measurement cost by using only two complementary measurements and achieves fast, accurate state reconstruction for large systems.

**Method.** The authors utilize Kirkwood-Dirac (KD) quasiprobability to formulate a state reconstruction problem, solved via a Complex Logistic Regression Estimator (CLRE) optimized with Projected Gradient Descent (PGD).

**Model / system.** The system is a general quantum state $\rho$ on a $d$-dimensional Hilbert space (e.g., $n$ qubits). The methodology is applied to reconstruct this unknown state from measurement statistics.

**Key observables.** Reconstructed state $\tilde{\rho}$, reconstruction fidelity $F(\rho_1, \rho_2)$, and the KD quasiprobability distribution $\{q_{ab}\}$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of qubits ($n$), the dimension $d=2^n$, and the ratio of measured observables to required observables ($K/d^2$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The protocol relies on the theoretical framework of KD quasiprobability and assumes the effectiveness of the CLRE as a practical estimator, despite its lack of direct physical interpretation.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare state infidelity vs. iteration (showing CLRE convergence speed vs. Pauli-MLE) and reconstruction fidelity vs. the ratio of measured observables to required observables ($K/d^2$).

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces QST and KD quasiprobability, demonstrates KD's suitability, proposes the CLRE estimator, details the PGD algorithm, analyzes computational complexity, and concludes with extensive experimental validation.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum state tomography (QST) is of fundamental importance to characterize quantum systems in quantum information processing, but its practical implementation is severely hindered by the exponential scaling of measurement and computational costs. In this paper, we present a novel QST protocol that utilizes Kirkwood-Dirac (KD) quasiprobability to reconstruct quantum states. First, it enables state reconstruction with only two complementary rank-one projective measurements, thus significantly reducing the measurement cost. Then, a complex logistic regression estimator is proposed to process collected KD data, together with a projected gradient algorithm to mitigate numerical instability and to accelerate convergence. The product-operator structure of KD quasiprobability is further exploited to reduce the computational cost. Finally, extensive experiments are implemented to confirm the validity of our protocol. Notably, the full reconstruction of randomly generated 15-qubit mixed-state instances can be accomplished within 20 minutes under the GPU implementation. These results suggest a promising route toward scalable QST and benchmarking large-scale quantum systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work demonstrates how engineering a superlattice on a Chern-insulator model can create a highly uniform miniband capable of hosting a fractional Chern insulator. By analyzing the competition between different correlated states using pseudospin anisotropy, the authors show a pathway to selectively control the ground state between a balanced FQSH-like state and a fully polarized FCI.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work provides a concrete, tunable lattice platform (superlattice) to realize and control multiple competing topological phases (FQSH vs. FCI), which is highly relevant for designing artificial quantum matter systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of engineering and controlling competing fractional topological states by combining band structure reconstruction, interaction-driven correlation effects, and external control mechanisms.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrate that applying a superlattice modulation to the QWZ model creates a narrow miniband hosting a $
u=1/3$ Fractional Chern Insulator (FCI), which, when paired with its time-reversed partner (BHZ), exhibits a competition between a balanced FQSH-like state and a fully polarized FCI.

**Method.** The study uses exact diagonalization on a projected interacting Hamiltonian derived from the superlattice-reconstructed single-particle band, supplemented by analysis of energy sector competition using pseudospin anisotropy.

**Model / system.** The system is based on the Qi-Wu-Zhang (QWZ) Chern-insulator model, modified by a scalar superlattice modulation to form a BHZ superlattice. The analysis focuses on the resulting isolated $C=+1$ miniband and its many-body physics at total filling $2/3$.

**Key observables.** Berry curvature ($\Omega$), quantum metric fluctuation ($\delta 	ext{Tr } g$), Chern number ($	ext{CMB}$), and the relative energies of competing polarization sectors ($E_P$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Total filling ($
u=2/3$), superlattice modulation strength ($V_0$), and the strength of the uniform pseudospin anisotropy ($g_z$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that the superlattice reconstruction successfully isolates the target miniband, and that the competition between states can be mapped onto the relative energy shifts governed by pseudospin anisotropy.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the superlattice reconstruction, showing the narrow, isolated target miniband and the reduction in geometric fluctuations. Figure 2 confirms the FCI nature via spectral flow and $	ext{CMB}=1$. Figure E1 details how uniform anisotropy shifts the energy of different polarization sectors, determining the ground state.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the physical model using a superlattice applied to the QWZ model. It then analyzes the single-particle reconstruction to confirm the formation of a uniform, isolated miniband. Subsequently, it performs many-body calculations to identify the $
u=1/3$ FCI, and finally, it analyzes the competition between different fractional states using the pseudospin anisotropy parameter.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Scalar superlattices offer a route from simple topological bands to fractionalized states, while multicomponent systems raise the additional question of which fractional order is energetically selected. We show that a scalar superlattice applied to the Qi-Wu-Zhang (QWZ) Chern-insulator model produces an isolated C = +1 miniband with strongly improved Berry-curvature and quantum metric uniformity. Exact diagonalization of the projected interaction identifies a 1/3 fractional Chern insulator in this miniband. Restoring the time-reversed partner to form the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang (BHZ) superlattice yields, at total filling 2/3, a balanced fractional quantum spin Hall (FQSH)-like state and a fully polarized 2/3 fractional Chern insulator. Their competition separates two aspects of fractional-state control: the finite-momentum intercomponent coupling governs the stability of the balanced FQSH-like state, whereas a uniform pseudospin anisotropy shifts the relative energies of conserved sectors and can switch the global ground state between the balanced and polarized states. These results establish a minimal lattice setting that connects topological-miniband reconstruction, fractional-state formation, and fractional-state selection, illustrating how distinct levels of control can be combined to navigate competing fractional topological states.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical study predicts that light passing through disordered ensembles of two-level emitters can violate a Bell inequality. The violation is found to occur in two distinct regimes—antibunched and bunched—depending on the number of emitters present. The analysis uses advanced techniques like fourth-order cumulant expansions applied to the system's master equation.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work connects fundamental quantum non-locality tests (Bell inequalities) to realistic solid-state quantum emitters, providing theoretical predictions for observable quantum correlations in disordered media.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the violation of Bell inequalities using light transmitted through disordered ensembles of weakly coupled two-level emitters.

**Main result.** Bell-inequality violations are predicted in two distinct regimes—an antibunched regime ($N \simeq 75-220$) and a bunched regime ($N \gtrsim 250$)—depending on the emitter density.

**Method.** The analysis employs a fourth-order cumulant expansion of the many-body master equation to calculate necessary output-field correlations.

**Model / system.** The system is a disordered ensemble of weakly coupled two-level emitters coupled to a 1D optical channel, modeled using the bidirectional waveguide model (BWM).

**Key observables.** Equal-time intensity correlation $g^{(2)}(0)$ and phase-sensitive two-photon coherence $R$, which determine the optimized CHSH parameter $S_{	ext{opt}}$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Single-emitter coupling $eta$, total decay rate $\Gamma_{	ext{tot}}$, and the total number of emitters $N$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The calculations rely on a fourth-order cumulant expansion of the master equation, and the analysis distinguishes between antibunched and bunched correlation regimes.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the experimental setup, show disorder-averaged observables ($g^{(2)}, R, S_{	ext{opt}}$) versus $N$, and map out the parameter space showing the existence of violation in both antibunched and bunched regimes.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the physical model via the master equation, derives the necessary correlation functions using cumulant expansions, predicts the existence of Bell violation in two distinct regimes, and quantifies the required emitter numbers for violation in each regime.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We show that light transmitted through a disordered ensemble of weakly coupled two-level emitters can violate a Bell inequality in a continuous-wave Franson-type measurement. The Bell signal is determined by two steady-state output-field correlations, the equal-time intensity correlation $g^{(2)}(0)$ and the phase-sensitive two-photon coherence $R$. We compute these quantities for bidirectional propagation through disordered emitter ensembles using a fourth-order cumulant expansion of the many-body master equation. The resulting Bell inequality violation appears in two distinct regimes, an antibunched regime where equal-time coincidences are suppressed and a bunched regime where photon pairs remain phase coherent. Extrapolating the numerics to a representative weak single-emitter coupling $β=0.01$ predicts violation in the antibunched regime for atom numbers $N\simeq75$-$220$, and in the bunched regime for $N\gtrsim250$.

</details>

**Summary.** This work investigates collective oscillations in nonreciprocal Ising spin networks, comparing theoretical approximations against detailed Monte Carlo simulations. The key finding is that while local interaction parameters are crucial, the macroscopic oscillatory behavior is fundamentally dictated by the network's geometry, as demonstrated by contrasting results on periodic versus edge-swapped lattices.

**Why it may be interesting.** The focus on non-equilibrium dynamics, collective oscillations, and the explicit comparison of local correlation approximations (NSC) to global behavior is highly relevant to open quantum systems and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to determine how local nonreciprocal interactions predict global collective oscillations in nonreciprocal Ising networks, and whether network geometry is the key determinant of these oscillations.

**Main result.** The paper finds that while local theories can predict oscillations on edge-swapped networks, the macroscopic behavior (amplitude and angular momentum) strongly depends on the underlying network geometry, showing a clear difference between periodic lattices and swapped ones.

**Method.** The authors compare three theoretical approximations (Mean-Field, Independent-Node, Nearest-Neighbor Spin-Coupling) against extensive Monte Carlo simulations on different network topologies.

**Model / system.** The system is a two-spin nonreciprocal Ising model defined on a connected undirected network, featuring nonreciprocal Glauber dynamics. The model is analyzed on both periodic square lattices and degree-preserving edge-swapped networks.

**Key observables.** Oscillation amplitude ($R_{rms}$), angular momentum ($L$), and period ($T$) are the primary global diagnostics used to characterize the collective dynamics.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Key parameters include the coupling strengths ($eta J, eta K^+, eta K^-$), the coordination number ($z=4$), system size ($L$), and the edge-swapping intensity ($f$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on comparing theoretical closures (MF, ID, NSC) against the full, non-equilibrium dynamics simulated via Monte Carlo methods.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the model setup, the comparison of theoretical predictions vs. MC results for $R_{rms}, L, T$ across different couplings, and finite-size scaling tests showing the divergence of behavior between square lattices and edge-swapped networks.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the model and comparing local theories (MF, ID, NSC) against MC simulations. It then performs finite-size scaling tests by comparing results on periodic lattices versus edge-swapped networks to isolate the role of geometry.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Nonreciprocal many-body dynamics can develop a swap phase characterized by spontaneous global oscillations far from equilibrium. To determine how local nonreciprocal interactions predict global oscillations and how broadly this prediction applies, we compare mean-field theory, independent-node theory, and nearest-neighbor spin-coupling theory for a two-spin nonreciprocal Ising model on networks of fixed coordination number (\(z=4\)). Nearest-neighbor spin-coupling theory retains nine independent joint edge probabilities. Monte Carlo benchmarks show that it predicts the oscillation amplitude, angular momentum, and period on edge-swapped networks with a 2.1\% aggregate mean absolute relative error. We then extend the square lattice to degree-preserving edge-swapped networks and find sharply different behavior. With increasing system size, the oscillation amplitude and angular momentum decay strongly on the periodic square lattice but remain nearly size independent on edge-swapped networks. These results show that identical local parameters do not determine the macroscopic phase. The contrasting finite-size trends identify network geometry as a key determinant of collective oscillations at fixed local interaction parameters.

</details>

**Summary.** This text provides a comprehensive theoretical framework for open quantum systems, detailing how environmental interaction causes decoherence and dissipation. It develops the necessary mathematical tools, such as the quantum master equation, to model the system's reduced dynamics. The work connects these quantum mechanical descriptions directly to fundamental principles of quantum thermodynamics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This is highly relevant as it provides the foundational theoretical tools (GKSL, reduced dynamics) necessary to model realistic quantum devices where environmental coupling is unavoidable, bridging quantum mechanics with thermodynamics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of describing quantum systems that interact unavoidably with their environment, focusing on understanding the physical origins of decoherence and dissipation.

**Main result.** It develops the theoretical framework using quantum master equations (GKSL) to model open quantum dynamics, connecting these processes to fundamental principles of quantum thermodynamics.

**Method.** The methodology involves deriving reduced dynamics by tracing out environmental degrees of freedom, utilizing the density matrix formalism, and applying approximations like the Born-Markov limit.

**Model / system.** The system is a general quantum system interacting with an environment. The dynamics are modeled using the Lindblad master equation, which governs the time evolution of the density matrix $\rho$. Specific examples include qubit dynamics and harmonic oscillators.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature ($T$), coupling strengths ($\gamma$), and characteristic time scales ($T_2$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumptions include the use of the Born-Markov approximation and the requirement of detailed balance for reaching thermal equilibrium.

**Figures summary.** The notes reference a Bloch sphere trajectory showing decay towards the center for qubit dynamics, and equations detailing heat and energy flow over time.

**Paper structure.** The structure progresses from reviewing closed system dynamics (Schrödinger/von Neumann) to introducing the open system challenge, deriving the GKSL equation, and finally applying the formalism to quantum thermodynamics laws (heat, work, entropy).

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Open quantum systems describe quantum systems that interact unavoidably with their environments. These notes introduce the physical origins of decoherence and dissipation in realistic settings, developing the theoretical framework of reduced dynamics and quantum master equations within the connection to thermodynamics in the quantum regime. Additionally, a set of relevant exercises are proposed to reinforce the acquisition of knowledge. The text equips readers with the tools to model and analyze open quantum dynamics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper rigorously defines the time-evolution of an SLH-network, resolving ambiguities in the initial definition related to the essential self-adjointness of the generator.

**Main result.** The braid map provides an unambiguous definition for the network, and the series product is shown to govern the time evolution in the instantaneous feed-forward limit.

**Method.** The authors employ quantum stochastic calculus, defining the evolution via a unitary cocycle and deriving the series product by taking the zero-delay limit of the cascaded system evolution.

**Model / system.** The model is an SLH-network, conceptualized as a cascade of quantum systems connected by feedback connections characterized by a time delay. The dynamics are governed by a unitary cocycle solving a Quantum Stochastic Differential Equation (QSDE).

**Key observables.** The time-evolution operator $\hat{U}_t$ and the resulting series product $V_t$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The time delay $\xi$, the network structure defined by the SLH-triple $(S, L, H)$, and the limit parameter $	au 	o 0$ (instantaneous feed-forward limit).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The initial definition was conditional on an open conjecture regarding essential self-adjointness, which the QSDE approach resolves.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the rigorous definition of the network evolution using the braid map. It then analyzes the time evolution for finite delay using a cocycle structure. Finally, it derives the series product by taking the limit of the cascaded evolution in the zero-delay limit.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

This article investigates a cascade of quantum systems within an SLH-network. The SLH-network is defined rigorously by using the so-called braid-map. **Summary.** This review unifies disparate fields—from classical control theory to modern machine learning—by showing they all rely on minimizing free-energy-like functionals. It establishes a deep mathematical link between optimal control, statistical inference, and non-equilibrium thermodynamics. This unified perspective offers a powerful new theoretical lens for analyzing complex physical and computational systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** The deep mathematical connections drawn between non-equilibrium thermodynamics (entropy production) and modern ML techniques (like flow matching) provide powerful new theoretical tools for analyzing open quantum systems and dissipation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper unifies five distinct fields—control theory, optimal transport, probabilistic inference, non-equilibrium thermodynamics, and machine learning—by identifying a common mathematical thread.

**Main result.** This thread centers on the optimization of free-energy-like functionals subject to dynamical or statistical constraints, providing a unified framework for understanding learning processes in physics.

**Method.** The authors employ variational principles, connecting optimal control formulations (Hamiltonian/Lagrangian mechanics) to density evolution via Wasserstein geometry and maximum entropy principles.

**Model / system.** The framework applies to general dynamical systems and stochastic processes, modeling state evolution $x_t$ under control $u_t$ or diffusion noise $\eta_t$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The review assumes the reader is comfortable with advanced mathematical concepts, moving from path-space to density-space descriptions.

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The last decade has seen the development of powerful methods for learning complex structure from high-dimensional data. These advances have brought to the foreground fundamental connections between subdisciplines of physics, applied mathematics, and machine learning. In this review, we bring together some of these ideas, often expressed in different languages, to highlight a conceptual thread that links five distinct fields: control theory, optimal transport, probabilistic inference, non-equilibrium thermodynamics, and machine learning. A common theme is the optimization of free-energy-like functionals under dynamical or statistical constraints. We offer a guided tour through this thread and present selected applications in reinforcement learning, variational inference, and generative modeling. The review does not assume prior familiarity with these topics, and begins with principles originating from physics.

</details>
